beats.beat: Owen asks Rowe plainly what his intentions are, since his sister's name is now in every kitchen in Amberlight.
Rowe, startled into honesty, admits he does not know what to call his feeling, only that it is slower and better than the gossip allows.
Word arrives that Louisa's uncle has agreed to fit the old east wing of Amberlight House as a schoolroom at the estate's expense, needing no subscription at all.
Rowe realizes that with the money settled, he has no more useful reason to marry, only whatever reason is left over, which is Judith herself.
He sets out to find her and meets her already on the road to his lodging, come to settle the matter of the gossip herself.

turn.note: Judith's declaration that she has come to settle the matter herself, and is not a thing to be settled between the two men, reframes chapter 7 as her scene rather than his.

continuity: Owen's confrontation begins immediately from Chapter 5's Monday afternoon ('half past three'), but Louisa then arrives having just read a letter she calls 'Tuesday's post' -- the bible states the coach runs only Tuesdays and Fridays, so a Tuesday delivery cannot have reached her on the same Monday scene.
trope_note: Serves the chaperone's-absence trope directly as fallout (Owen's confrontation, the gossip) and keeps the enemies-of-manner banter alive through the schoolroom exchange; no fourth trope is introduced.
fixes: Cut the repetition of 'black coat' and 'neckcloth' across two consecutive narrator paragraphs (segments 16 and 17) -- keep it in one place.
Shorten the opening tally of subscription sums (nine shillings, straw, four shillings) since the fifteen-pound figure and its shortfall were already established in Chapters 1 and 3.
Fix the timeline: either move Louisa's letter to the following day or change 'Tuesday's post' to match the same-day continuation from Owen's Monday visit.
Trim the ambient description of the green in 'It was not raining... nothing better to look at' -- the coach-and-crowd image was already used to close Chapter 4.
Condense the description of Judith at the lych gate ('bonnet on straight and her chin up...') to fewer clauses; the point can be made in one image.
Remove the doubled spaces after 'his neck.' and 'open the shop.' -- likely stray formatting, not intended emphasis.
